tips.title: FSH matures, LH releases
tips.body: **F**SH makes the egg **f**orm; **L**H **l**ets it go. If you remember nothing else about the four hormones, remember this — it is the pair most often swapped, and both appear in almost every question on the cycle.

tips.title: Two from the pituitary, two from the ovary
tips.body: **FSH and LH** come from the **pituitary** and act on the **ovary**. **Oestrogen and progesterone** come from the **ovary** and act on the **uterus** — and back on the pituitary. Splitting them that way halves what there is to learn.

tips.title: Give oestrogen all three effects
tips.body: It thickens the lining, **inhibits FSH**, and **stimulates LH**. Most answers give only the first. The other two are the feedback that makes it a cycle, and they are where the 7.5 marks actually are.

tips.title: The pill works by keeping FSH low
tips.body: High oestrogen and progesterone **inhibit FSH**, so **no egg matures**. That one sentence answers every *how does hormonal contraception work* question, and it connects the contraception marks to the feedback marks.

tips.title: Evaluate means both sides, then judge
tips.body: Effectiveness, infection, side effects, convenience — two points each way, then a judgement. For contraception the strongest judgement is that a condom **with** a hormonal method gives both the reliability and the STI protection.

why.matters:
Four hormones, two glands and about twenty-eight days, arranged so that an egg is released at roughly the moment the uterus lining is ready for it. Nothing is in charge: each hormone triggers the next and then the levels themselves switch things off.

Which is why the same four hormones can be used to **prevent** pregnancy and to **help achieve** it. Contraception and fertility treatment are not different biology — they are the same loop, pushed in opposite directions.

examples.title: What is happening on which day
examples.body:
The cycle runs about **28 days** and ovulation sits near the middle, around day 14 — which is the fact the rest of the topic hangs on.

Before it, **FSH** matures a follicle and the **oestrogen** that follicle releases rebuilds the uterus lining. Oestrogen rising far enough triggers a surge of **LH**, and that surge is what causes ovulation. After it, the remains of the follicle release **progesterone**, which maintains the lining. If no embryo arrives, progesterone falls and the lining is shed.

visual.alt: A table of the menstrual cycle: menstruation over days one to five, the lining rebuilding from five to fourteen, ovulation at about day fourteen, and the lining maintained from fourteen to twenty-eight

examples.title: Why the pill works by pretending
examples.body:
Hormonal contraception contains oestrogen and progesterone, which sounds like the wrong idea until you follow the feedback. Kept **high**, both of them inhibit the release of **FSH** from the pituitary.

No FSH means no follicle matures, and no follicle means no egg to release. The body is not being blocked — it is being told, chemically, that a cycle is already well under way. Progesterone also thickens the mucus at the cervix, which is a second barrier working by an entirely different route.

visual.alt: A flow chart of hormonal contraception: oestrogen and progesterone kept high inhibit the release of FSH from the pituitary, so no follicle matures and no egg is released

examples.title: The same hormones, used the other way
examples.body:
If keeping FSH down prevents ovulation, then someone who does not ovulate regularly can often be helped by pushing FSH **up**. That is what **clomifene therapy** does.

**IVF** goes further: FSH and LH are given to mature several eggs at once, the eggs are collected and fertilised outside the body, and an embryo is put back. The hormones are the same ones in the cycle, and the whole difference between a contraceptive and a fertility treatment is which way the loop is pushed.

visual.alt: A table showing the same hormone pushed both ways: the pill suppresses FSH so that no egg is released, clomifene raises it to cause ovulation, and IVF raises it further so that several eggs can be collected

steps.title: The four stages of the cycle
steps.body:
The **menstrual cycle** takes about **28 days**, though it varies between people. Four things happen in it, and knowing what happens on roughly which day makes the hormones much easier to follow.

**Days 1 to 5 — menstruation.** The **lining of the uterus breaks down** and is lost. Day 1 of the cycle is the first day of bleeding, which is worth noting: the cycle is counted from the start of a period, not from ovulation.

**Days 5 to 14 — repair and thickening.** The lining is **rebuilt** and thickens, so that it could receive a fertilised egg.

**Day 14 — ovulation.** An **egg is released** from an ovary. This is a single day in the middle of the cycle.

**Days 14 to 28 — maintenance.** The lining is **maintained** in case the egg is fertilised. If it is not, the hormone keeping the lining in place falls away, the lining breaks down, and day 1 of the next cycle begins.

So the whole cycle is about preparing the uterus for a possible pregnancy, and starting again if there is not one.

steps.title: The four hormones
steps.body:
Four hormones control the cycle, and they come from **two** places. Splitting them that way makes them far easier to hold:

**From the pituitary gland** (the master gland, in the brain):

- **FSH** — follicle stimulating hormone. It causes an **egg to mature** in the ovary, and stimulates the ovaries to produce **oestrogen**.
- **LH** — luteinising hormone. It causes **ovulation**: the mature egg is released.

**From the ovaries**:

- **Oestrogen** — it causes the lining of the uterus to **repair and thicken**. It also **inhibits FSH** and **stimulates the release of LH**.
- **Progesterone** — it **maintains** the lining of the uterus. It **inhibits both FSH and LH**.

Notice the pattern: the **pituitary hormones act on the ovary**, and the **ovarian hormones act on the uterus — and back on the pituitary**. That feedback is what makes it a cycle rather than a one-way sequence.

A memory hook for the names: **F**SH makes the egg **f**orm; **L**H **l**ets it go.

steps.title: Hormonal contraception
steps.body:
**Hormonal contraception** uses **oestrogen and/or progesterone** to prevent pregnancy, and it works by exploiting the feedback you have just met.

**How it works.** Both ovarian hormones **inhibit FSH**. Keeping their level artificially high therefore keeps FSH low — so **no egg matures**, and **no ovulation** occurs. Progesterone also **thickens the mucus at the cervix**, making it harder for sperm to get through.

That is the key sentence for the exam: *it keeps FSH low, so no egg matures*.

**The forms it comes in:**

- the **pill**, taken daily
- an **implant** under the skin, lasting years
- an **injection**, lasting months
- a **patch** worn on the skin

The longer-lasting forms exist for a practical reason: the pill only works if it is taken **every day**, and forgetting is the commonest way it fails.

**Barrier methods** work completely differently. A **condom** or a **diaphragm** physically **stops the sperm reaching the egg** — no hormones are involved and the cycle is unchanged.

And one difference matters a great deal: a **condom also protects against sexually transmitted infections**. No hormonal method does.

steps.title: Hormones and fertility treatment
steps.body:
The same hormones can be used to help someone become pregnant. Spec point 7.8 names two treatments.

**Clomifene therapy.** Some people do not **ovulate regularly**, often because they do not release enough FSH and LH. Clomifene is a drug that causes **more FSH and LH to be released**, so an egg **matures and is released**. It is taken around the time of the cycle when ovulation would normally occur.

**IVF — in vitro fertilisation.** *In vitro* means *in glass*: fertilisation happens outside the body.

1. **FSH and LH** are given, so that **several eggs mature** at once rather than one.
2. The eggs are **collected** from the ovaries.
3. They are **fertilised** in a laboratory using the partner's or a donor's **sperm**.
4. The fertilised eggs develop into **embryos**.
5. When they are tiny balls of cells, **one or two are inserted into the uterus**.

Note which hormones do which job, because it is a common slip: **clomifene makes the body release its own FSH and LH**, whereas in **IVF the hormones themselves are given** to mature several eggs at once.

**Evaluating IVF** is a standard question, and it wants both sides. It allows people who could not otherwise conceive to have a child. But it is **emotionally and physically stressful**, the **success rate is not high**, it is **expensive**, and putting back more than one embryo can lead to **multiple births**, which carry more risk to both babies and mother.

steps.title: Going deeper: the feedback, and how to evaluate
steps.body:
**Where the hard marks are.** Spec point 7.5 asks for the **interactions**, and the interactions are the feedback effects — the parts that act back on the pituitary rather than on the uterus:

- **Oestrogen inhibits FSH.** So once the lining is being built, no further eggs start to mature.
- **Oestrogen stimulates LH.** Rising oestrogen is what triggers the LH surge, and therefore ovulation. The cycle times itself.
- **Progesterone inhibits FSH and LH.** After ovulation, nothing more is released.

An answer that gives only the uterus effects — *oestrogen thickens the lining, progesterone maintains it* — has described half the system. The inhibition is what makes it a **cycle**.

It is also what makes the **pill** work, and being able to join those two facts is the mark of a top answer: *the pill keeps oestrogen and progesterone high, which keeps FSH low, so no egg matures.* The contraceptive is using the body's own feedback against itself.

**How to evaluate contraception.** *Evaluate* means give points on **both sides** and then reach a **judgement**. A useful frame:

- **Effectiveness** — hormonal methods are very effective **when used correctly**; the qualification matters, since forgetting a pill is the usual failure.
- **Infection** — only a **condom** protects against STIs. This is often the deciding point, and it is the one most answers miss.
- **Side effects** — hormonal methods can cause them; barrier methods do not.
- **Convenience** — an implant lasts years and needs no thought; a condom must be used every time.

A judgement might be that **using both together** gives the effectiveness of one and the infection protection of the other — which is a better answer than declaring one method best.

**Two distinctions worth keeping straight.**

- **FSH matures, LH releases.** If you can only remember one, remember that.
- **Clomifene** makes the body release **its own** FSH and LH; in **IVF** the hormones are **given directly**. Both involve the same two hormones, for different purposes.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- The cycle is about **28 days**: **menstruation** (1–5), **repair and thickening** (5–14), **ovulation** (about day 14), **maintenance** (14–28).
- Day 1 is the **first day of bleeding**.
- **FSH** (pituitary): an egg **matures**, and the ovary is stimulated to make **oestrogen**.
- **LH** (pituitary): causes **ovulation**.
- **Oestrogen** (ovary): the lining **repairs and thickens**; it **inhibits FSH** and **stimulates LH**.
- **Progesterone** (ovary): the lining is **maintained**; it **inhibits FSH and LH**.
- **FSH matures, LH releases.**
- If the egg is not fertilised, **progesterone falls**, the lining **breaks down**, and the next cycle begins.
- **Hormonal contraception** keeps oestrogen and progesterone high, so **FSH stays low** and **no egg matures**. Progesterone also thickens cervical mucus.
- **Barrier methods** physically stop sperm reaching the egg, and a **condom also protects against STIs**.
- **Clomifene** makes the body release **more of its own FSH and LH**, so an egg matures and is released.
- **IVF**: FSH and LH are **given** so several eggs mature; they are collected, fertilised in a lab, and **one or two embryos** are inserted into the uterus.
- To **evaluate**, give points on both sides — effectiveness, infection, side effects, convenience — then judge.

questions.prompt: Explain how FSH, oestrogen, LH and progesterone interact to control the menstrual cycle, including the repair of the uterus wall, ovulation and menstruation.
questions.solution: FSH is released by the pituitary gland. It causes an egg to mature inside the ovary and stimulates the ovary to produce oestrogen. Oestrogen causes the lining of the uterus to repair and thicken so that it could receive a fertilised egg. Oestrogen also acts back on the pituitary gland, where it inhibits the release of further FSH, so that no more eggs begin to mature, and stimulates the release of LH. The resulting rise in LH causes ovulation, which is the release of the mature egg from the ovary, at about day fourteen. After ovulation the ovary produces progesterone, which maintains the thickened lining of the uterus in case the egg is fertilised. Progesterone also inhibits both FSH and LH, so no further eggs mature or are released during that cycle. If the egg is not fertilised, the level of progesterone falls. The lining can then no longer be maintained, so it breaks down and is lost as menstruation, and the fall in progesterone also removes the inhibition on FSH so that the next cycle can begin.

questions.modelAnswer:
**FSH** is released by the **pituitary**. It causes an **egg to mature** in the ovary and stimulates the ovary to produce **oestrogen**.

**Oestrogen** causes the uterus lining to **repair and thicken**. It also acts **back on the pituitary**: it **inhibits FSH**, so no further eggs begin to mature, and **stimulates the release of LH**.

**LH** rises and causes **ovulation** — the release of the mature egg — at about day 14.

The ovary then produces **progesterone**, which **maintains** the thickened lining in case the egg is fertilised, and **inhibits both FSH and LH** so nothing further is released this cycle.

If the egg is **not fertilised**, **progesterone falls**. The lining can no longer be maintained, so it **breaks down** and is lost — **menstruation**. The fall also removes the inhibition on FSH, so the next cycle can begin.

The marks that separate answers here are the **feedback** ones: oestrogen inhibiting FSH and stimulating LH, and progesterone inhibiting both. An answer that gives only the effects on the uterus has described half the system.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the use of hormonal and barrier methods of contraception.
questions.solution: Hormonal methods, such as the pill, the implant, the injection and the patch, work by keeping the levels of oestrogen and progesterone high, which inhibits FSH so that no egg matures and ovulation does not occur. They are very effective when they are used correctly, and longer lasting forms such as the implant require no daily action, which removes the commonest cause of failure. However, the pill has to be taken every day and forgetting it is the usual reason it fails, hormonal methods can cause side effects, and crucially none of them gives any protection against sexually transmitted infections. Barrier methods, such as the condom and the diaphragm, work by physically preventing the sperm from reaching the egg. They do not change the menstrual cycle and have no hormonal side effects, and a condom also protects against sexually transmitted infections, which is a significant advantage. They are somewhat less effective in practice because they can tear or slip, and they must be used correctly every time. Overall, neither method is simply better than the other. Hormonal methods are the more reliable at preventing pregnancy, while only a condom protects against infection, so using a condom together with a hormonal method gives both advantages at once.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Hormonal methods** — the pill, implant, injection, patch.

- **How they work:** keeping oestrogen and progesterone high **inhibits FSH**, so **no egg matures** and ovulation does not occur.
- **For:** very effective **when used correctly**; the implant and injection need no daily action.
- **Against:** the pill must be taken **every day**, and forgetting is the usual failure; possible **side effects**; **no protection against STIs**.

**Barrier methods** — condom, diaphragm.

- **How they work:** they physically **stop sperm reaching the egg**. The cycle is unchanged.
- **For:** no hormonal side effects, and a **condom protects against STIs**.
- **Against:** somewhat less effective in practice — they can tear or slip — and must be used correctly **every time**.

**The judgement.** Neither is simply better. Hormonal methods are more **reliable at preventing pregnancy**; only a **condom** protects against **infection**. So using a condom **together with** a hormonal method gives both advantages at once.

That last point is what makes it an evaluation rather than a comparison: the question asks you to weigh them, and the strongest answer notices they are not mutually exclusive.

examTechnique.body:
Work through the cycle in day order and each hormone appears where it is needed.

Name where each hormone is made as well as what it does. FSH and LH from the pituitary, oestrogen and progesterone from the ovary.

For spec point 7.5 give the feedback effects, not just the effects on the uterus. Oestrogen inhibits FSH and stimulates LH; progesterone inhibits both.

For contraception, say how the method works before listing advantages. Hormonal methods keep FSH low so no egg matures; barrier methods stop sperm reaching the egg.

When a question says evaluate, give points on both sides and then a judgement. Include the STI point, which most answers miss.

Keep clomifene and IVF apart: clomifene makes the body release its own FSH and LH, while IVF supplies them.
examinerErrors: Swapping FSH and LH, so that FSH is said to cause ovulation.
Saying oestrogen maintains the lining, which is progesterone's job.
Giving only the uterus effects of oestrogen and leaving out the feedback.
Saying the pill prevents the sperm reaching the egg, which is a barrier method.
Claiming a hormonal method protects against sexually transmitted infections.
Saying progesterone rises when the egg is not fertilised, when it falls.
Confusing clomifene with IVF, saying clomifene supplies hormones directly.
Listing advantages only when the question says evaluate.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer describes the cycle as a **loop** rather than a list: it gives the feedback effects on the pituitary, and can then explain the contraceptive pill as the body's own feedback used against itself. It keeps the four hormones straight by remembering where each is made, so it never has FSH coming from an ovary. Asked to evaluate, it gives points on both sides, includes the infection point that most answers miss, and reaches a judgement — noticing that the two kinds of method can be used together rather than treating the choice as either-or.
